utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Tuesday, the 23rd of February, 2010, I wish, first of all, to bid good morning to General Petkovic, also the accused present, ladies and gentlemen, members of the counsels, all the members of the OTP, and principally Madam West, and all the persons assisting us. Mr. Scott let us know yesterday that he would be absent and that he would be replaced by Mr. Stringer and Madam West. I should first like to render an oral decision, recalling the scope of the additional investigation. At the hearing of the 18th of February, 2010, the Prosecution requested from the Chamber that it clarify the scope of the re-examination. The Prosecution noted that on several occasions the Petkovic Defence had announced, during the examination-in-chief, that it did not wish to raise important issues related to the questions posed by the Judges during the examination-in-chief, but that it would address those issues during the re-examination. The Chamber recalls its decision of the 28th of April, 2006, regarding the adoption of guide-lines relating to the conduct of the proceedings, and another of the 24th of April, 2008, regarding guide-lines for the presentation of exculpatory material as a result of which the re-examination is limited to the points on which the cross-examination is related. Consequently, the Petkovic Defence is not authorised to address subjects other than those raised during the cross-examination during the re-examination. Nevertheless, the Chamber finds that regarding the subjects raised during the questions put by the Judges to Milivoj Petkovic at the end of the examination-in-chief and before the cross-examination by the other parties, they may -- if it is so required, and upon approval by the Chamber, these questions may be raised by the Petkovic Defence. This means that when judges raise questions which were not raised during the examination-in-chief, the Petkovic Defence may, upon permission of the Chamber, during the re-examination raise those issues. By way of an example, the question of forced labour. I think it is clear now. Similarly, a further point of precision. The Chamber told the Praljak Defence that they have a week, upon the receipt of the translation into English of the order on the admission of exhibits, to raise possible requests for leave to appeal, but this also applies to all the other parties. It applies to the Prosecution and to the other Defence counsels. Once you have the English translation, you will all have a week. By way of an example, I'm going to try and complete my differing opinion on the admission of evidence, and it consists of six pages. Until it is translated, you will have seven days after you receive the translation of my dissenting opinion. So you will have all the elements for a motion for certification and right to appeal. I thank the Petkovic Defence for providing me this morning with a complete table of the documents which I will refer to when asking questions of General Petkovic. I relied basically on all the documents appearing in this so-called opening statement. And after review, it appears there are 29, in fact, documents that were not presented during the examination-in-chief, which means that I'm going to remove them from the list of the second day. I'm going to indicate which they are, and I tell you. I will not be referring to 3D02270, P01336, 4D0075, 4D01078, 3D00036, 4D00321, 4D00312, 4D00864, 4D00863, P03030, 3D03126, P03746, 4D00519, 4D00566, 3D0036, 3D02270, 3D03126 -- wait a moment. Apparently I repeated the same document -- 4D00437, 4D0079, 4D863, 4D864, 4D01078, 4D01520, P01336, P03030, P03303, and P03746. In any event, I shall bear in mind Ms. Alaburic's documents. I wanted to say that I was prompted to do this because I did exactly the same for the documents of the Prosecution. I realised that there were documents that were not referred to, so I have not included them in my list. And I shall do the same for the documents of the Petkovic Defence. In any event, I wish to say the following: Regarding Rule 16 of the Statute, under the heading "The Prosecutor," it says: "The Prosecutor is responsible for the formation of the brief." The term "brief" was introduced by the Statute. When I arrived at this Tribunal, there was a plenary session, and Judge May, who chaired the Milosevic case, during this plenary session proposed to the standing Judges, the permanent Judges, to introduce into the Rules this notion of a brief, and he explained that for him the brief consisted -- the file consisted of various documents. There was a debate at the plenary meeting, and his proposal was not followed; it was rejected. I, myself, being quite new at the Tribunal, I took the position and said, No, there shouldn't be a file or a brief because the evidence is produced by the parties. Now, if such proposal had been made, I would have had a different opinion, because the term "file" appears in the Statute, and there are files or briefs. And if there are files, then there is also evidence in those files. And due to this, it was necessary to regulate all the questions of the evidence during the pre-trial rather than during the trial itself, because this takes up an enormous amount of time. So perhaps other tribunals will address this problem. But as far as we are concerned, we are in a situation when the evidence that is admitted is admitted at the end of the testimony of witnesses or within the guide-lines. Therefore, I cannot use a document which has not been produced at a given point in time, even if that document may be of interest. Of course, in the interests of justice, I may be prompted to raise this, but this could produce other problems. That is why I'm going to withdraw certain documents from my initial list. And, furthermore, this will help us to save time, so I'm going to try to speed things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, yesterday I told you that I would complete with my consideration of the indictment with the four following paragraphs: "Milivoj Petkovic promoted, facilitated, and encouraged the joint criminal enterprise by casting Bosnian Muslims in a negative light by referring to them in derogatory terms in orders and communications to the Herceg-Bosna HVO Armed Forces." General, what is your comment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this courtroom you have had an opportunity of seeing hundreds of documents signed by me, and you were able to see only one document where this is mentioned. What I can say is this: I'm not the author of that document, but I am the signatory of the document. And I'm not going to defend myself from that fact. Had it been my intention, then you would have found that in any number of documents. However, at a point in time, it so happened that I put my signature to a document like that. It was not my intention, nor was it my position. I did not insult a nation, an ethnic group. And in that document -- I signed it without looking at the document, and I think that you'll find that that is the only document of that kind in hundreds of other documents. And as such, I don't think it reflects what the Prosecutor wants to ascribe to me and hold me responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Small (m): "It was up to Milivoj Petkovic to make sure that the forces of the HVO respect the Geneva Conventions and International Humanitarian Law, and that all detained prisoners and other persons should be treated in accordance with these conventions and the International Humanitarian Law." What is your comment, General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, similarly through these proceedings in this trial, you could see many orders signed by me on behalf of the Main Staff, because my subordinates were asked to implement the Geneva Conventions, and I claim that by no document of Herceg-Bosna, or act, was I responsible, as chief of the Main Staff or any of my commands, for detention centres. Nobody ever called me to attend any discussion, whether at government level or anywhere else, where detention centres are mentioned. Nobody gave me any responsibilities or tasks or assignments in that regard. I did not take part, either me or the Main Staff, or anybody from the Main Staff, when such detention centres were being disbanded, dismantled. Therefore, I consider that one -- no document from Herceg-Bosna ever bound me or the Main Staff as having that duty, and I claim that it was in no way a task of the Main Staff of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Small (n): "Milivoj Petkovic participated in, facilitated, instigated, encouraged, and condoned crimes and abuses against Bosnian Muslims by Herceg-Bosna HVO forces, by failing to prevent and punish such crimes and by commending, rewarding, promoting, or leaving in place HVO officers and soldiers who committed or played a role in such crimes." What do you say in response to this paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I claim that I did not fail to act, as the Prosecutor claims, with respect to these crimes. During this trial, you could see orders where I asked for responsibility and accountability at certain levels. In this courtroom, we were able to see some orders and parts of orders where I suggest that, on threat of force, certain individuals must be placed under supervision and control. Furthermore, on the basis of the law and regulations, which one could read again, did not have the authority that the Prosecutor ascribes to me. I did not appoint commanders of a certain rank. I did not relieve of duty commanders of a certain rank. And I don't remember ever commending or rewarding anybody. And I think that I did ask for certain measures to be taken, specifically whereby certain commands should be reorganised completely, that certain commanders leave their posts, whether it be in Prozor, or whether they were measures that were called for in Vakuf, and some measures that were implemented in Mostar in such a way as having certain senior commanding officers leave their posts and positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will finish with paragraph (o), which I'm going to read: "Milivoj Petkovic directed, participated in, and facilitated the concealment of crimes committed by Herceg-Bosna HVO forces in, by way of example, ordering in August 1993 that Bosnian Muslim detainees held in Prozor be made presentable before allowing international observers to see them, and misrepresenting and covering up crimes committed by Herceg-Bosna HVO forces at Stupni Do in October 1993." General Petkovic, your comment with regard to these last charges attributed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the free entry of the International Red Cross Committee into all the facilities that they asked to visit, without any restrictions or procedure, means that nothing was being hidden from anybody. At a point in time, it is quite normal, if somebody announces a visit, that you take a look at the people that are going to be visited; that you talk to them, that you tell them that there would be a visit, so button up your shirts, tighten your belts, that kind of thing, let's see whether you have put the place you slept in in order. So that's something that any soldier would do and is expected of a soldier. And let me tell you that in this particular Detention Unit where I am at present, when there's a visit, we would be told, Please put your facilities in order. So I think that is quite justified and very human, and nothing was upset by that. Now, the serious consequences two or three hours later cannot be covered up or hidden in any way before the ICRC turned up. Now, as far as Stupni Do is concerned, I say with full responsibility here that through issuing my order, I secured the entry of UNPROFOR forces into Stupni Do, and thereby I automatically ensured that the news of Stupni Do should be disseminated to all four corners of the world so that all the important factors in the international community be informed about it. I also ensured that the scene was protected and secured. And, similarly, I took measures to see that the United Nations and their forces should have the necessary conditions to carry out an investigation and that the United Nations should be informed thereof. And all structures in Herceg-Bosna as well, they were all informed with the fact, including the political leadership of the Republic of Croatia. And I do not see in what way it is alleged that this was covered up or hidden from anyone. It was accessible to one and all, everybody who wanted to get to know the situation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To finish with the indictment, I should like to hear your comments following the confirmation that you gave me yesterday of the fact that you were never interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor either as a witness or as a suspect, and it was only when the indictment was issued in 2004 that you learnt that you have been accused. I thought over what you told me yesterday, that you had never been interviewed, and I will give you some elements and I would like you to answer the questions I'm going to put to you. I looked at all the names in figuring in the joint criminal enterprise and when they were accused by an indictment for such facts or similar facts. For example, Bobetko, there was an indictment issued on the 17th of September, 2002. And then, as he is dead, nothing happened. Blaskic, the indictment issued the 10th of November, 1995, the judgement of the 3rd of March, 2000, that was the first-level judgement. Cerkez, 10th of November, 1995, the first-instance judgement 26th of November, 2001. Naletilic, indictment 21st of September, 1998; judgement, 31st of December, 2003. Rajic, Ivica, indictment 29th of October, 1995; judgement, 8th of May, 2006. And your own indictment was issued at the beginning of 2004. How would you explain, General Petkovic, that when you may have been the superior of some of the persons who were accused, with the exception of General Bobetko - I leave him aside - that you, yourself, were indicted many years later? Do you see any explanation, or is there none, according to you, for this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't know how -- or what explanation I could give, because everything you have put forward, I followed, and I expected that somebody from the Prosecution would ask at least to talk to me, if nothing else. As you said, there were four or five people here who were in the structure of the Croatian Defence Council. However, that never came about. And then what I happened to hear, allegedly, was that there was an about-turn and that it was said, Leave all those down there and catch the highest levels. And so probably that's what they decided to do in their selection of bringing the six of us in here. Up until then, nobody talked to me at no point, nobody said a single word to me, nor did they ask my assistance in any way, nor did anybody ask me to be a witness, for example, a Prosecution witness or anything like that. And it would appear that nobody came into contact with me until 2004, when something was obviously happening here and when it was decided to move ahead and start with the top. So this was probably politically motivated. Well, that's my position, anyway. I can't say any more than that. I did expect -- I really did expect somebody from the OTP to contact me in one way or another. However, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So, General Petkovic, as I said yesterday, we'll have a look at two videos, but for technical reasons alone. The first one is P08987. Would the Registrar do what is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, we have a technical problem. The Legal Officer could perhaps discuss the matter with the Registrar. The second video I wanted to show is IC00574. We can go back to that when it's possible. We won't waste any more time. The Legal Officer will tell me when it will be possible to view the videos. I would now like document P09276 to be shown, 276. Could we have it up on the screen, please. I would like to see the map 0504-5502, Map number 9, on the ethnic composition. Very well. General Petkovic, you can see the ethnic composition of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 in front of you, municipalities with a Serbian majority in red, places with Croats in blue, et cetera. We won't go into the details of the ethnic composition, but what I would like to know is: As of the events of 1992 and the events at the beginning of 1993, from that time onwards, given that there were all those refugees present, would you say that the ethnic composition changed completely as a result of the fact that refugees would leave one area and move to a different area? Do you have any examples you could provide us with?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In certain places, the relationship was completely changed. In other places, there was an increase of certain peoples. What is represented in red, for example, in the western part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is an area which was under the control of the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska at the time. Most of the people from those areas, from Banja Luka and from the surrounding municipalities, went to Central Bosnia, and many went to the Republic of Croatia. When they arrived in the area of Central Bosnia, it's quite certain that the ethnic composition had to change. Similarly, the part represented in red to the east of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that part also changed. People moved to the central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and forces massed there. And unfortunately because of expulsions and so on and so forth, the Bosniaks and Muslims prevailed there. From the western area, there were quite a few Croats. About 200.000 Croats went from the western part under the control of the Serbs, or, rather, they were expelled from that part and they left that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, the Prosecution has a theory that concerns these migrations. They say that by expelling Muslims who lived in certain areas, you managed to establish Croatian majorities, in particular, in Provinces 3, 8, and 10, in those areas. You participated in meetings in Geneva. You know what Provinces 3, 8, and 10 mean. So what is your opinion with regard to this thesis, these claims, according to which, by expelling or detaining Muslims, or by making them go abroad or elsewhere, one managed to establish areas where Croats were in the majority? That was done for the sake of the future.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Province number 3, that's the Posavina area to the north, but it isn't as depicted here by the Prosecution, it's just a small area around Orasje, on the whole the Croats were in the majority there, and that didn't change from October 1992, after the Serbian forces had taken all these municipalities that the Prosecution claims belonged to the Bosnian Posavina. It's true that was the case at the beginning, but by October they were all under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, apart from Orasje municipality and perhaps from a small part of the municipality of Odrid [phoen] and Bosanski Brod. And in that area, the Croats were mostly in the majority. As far as Province 10 is concerned, that's the Muslim area, in that area the Croatian population wasn't really in the majority because prior to that the red part to the east of Bosnia and Herzegovina, from Kalinovik, Nevesinje, Dracko [phoen], Bilica, and Ljubinje municipalities, all the expelled Muslims from these areas found a place to go to in the area from Jablanica, Konjic, and mostly in Mostar, and in areas in the direction of Capljina or Stolac. So when the Muslims arrived who had been expelled from Eastern Herzegovina, there were a significant number of Muslims in that area, in those areas. And nothing indicates that the number of Croats in these areas were significantly increased in relation to the number of Muslims. As far as Central Bosnia is concerned, when the Muslims and Croats were first expelled from western Bosnia under the control of the Serbs, while the Croats were -- left mostly for the Republic of Croatia, and many Muslims left with them, too, a lot of Muslims from that area, the Krajina Muslims, inhabited places from Zenica towards the central part of the Lasvansko-Lepenica Valley, and thus the structure was changed, the composition was completely changed. Especially when Jajce, the town of Jajce fell, then all the Muslims who had been expelled remained in Central Bosnia, whereas the Croats went -- some of them went to Herzegovina, but most of them to the Republic of Croatia. The central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, well, even before no one was really in the majority, but now the situation was such that the relationship was -- or the ratio was 2:1, and the Muslims were in the majority. They had been expelled from these areas, and they were in the Zenica-Vitez area and the Lasva-Lepenica Valley area, and that's how the situation remained. Towards the end of 1993, they remained there. In 80 per cent of the cases, they remained there, because the Croats from Travnik and Kakanj and Vares and Fojnica, Bugojno, they quite simply disappeared from those areas. When the HVO [as interpreted] launched its offensive, they were expelled. So towards the end of 1993 in the area of Central Bosnia, there was a concentration of Croats only in Vitez municipality, Busovaca municipality, in Kiseljak, and Kresevo municipalities. In other areas outside of these municipalities throughout Central Bosnia, we didn't have any Croats, apart from to the north in the territory of Zepce municipality. I'm not including the Croats who remained and who weren't affected by the 2nd Corps of the ABiH. I'm referring to the wider Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'd just like to correct the transcript. Page 14, line 17, the general spoke about an offensive of the ABiH and not of the HVO, which is what it says here. And this is an offensive that resulted in the expulsion of Croats from the towns that the general mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite right. I'm surprised that the contrary has been noted. The offensive of the ABiH launched against the towns in Central Bosnia, and several thousand Croats were expelled from those areas, and 80 per cent of the area was then inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Registrar now show the first video, P08987.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet, apparently. We'll have a look at the following document, P09234. General Petkovic, it's a depiction of the links that you had with Mr. Stojic or Mr. Boban, and above all it concerns the composition of your headquarters. As far as the links to Mr. Stojic are concerned, do you agree with what is stated? It says "Political and administrative authority," in relation to you.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Executive authority, Ministry of Defence." The Defence Department, it was part of the executive authority of the HVO, as one of its bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a civilian -- or, rather, there was a political control over the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among those who worked in the Main Staff, one can see the names, positions, et cetera. What I'm interested in is the Operations Centre. There's no name there, but I have the impression that it functioned 24 hours a day. Is this Operations Centre a centre that monitored all military activities in the field?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the operative centre -- Operations Centre was room in which there were three people on duty. They were together, and they maintained communication with certain units. Otherwise, the Operations Centre was not the unit to supervise combat, as it says here, combat activity, to oversee combat activity. What it does was to oversee and monitor all events in the operative zones. They need not be only combat activity. They oversee everything, the life and work, and everything that is reported to the Operations Centre. It compiles reports for a given day, and then everybody knows what was done in a certain zone. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you a specific case, Sovici and Doljani. In the organigram that we have, who followed the events there minute by minute?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sovici and Doljani, as well as everything else that was happening in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, was monitored by people who were on duty on that day in the Main Staff, and that would be three or four men who were designated to be connected to the communications equipment all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this duty, where is it on the organigram that we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all comes under the box as -- entitled "Operations Centre." In those days, there was no Operations Centre, as such. It was formed after the Main Staff moved to Citluk. Here, we had a duty service which would be linked to a telephone line in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, regardless of the combat going on on the ground, at all times at the level of the Main Staff you were informed of what may be happening. Is that correct or is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it all depended on whether it was the operative zone and how frequently it contacted the Main Staff. The Main Staff could not establish links with the situation on the ground, but only through the operative zone. So if the operative zone has information important for the Main Staff, it would pass it on. If not, they would call up in the morning, a few hours later, and then once again in the early evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll come back to Stupni Do through other documents. I'd now like to focus on Stupni Do, itself. Mr. Rajic was in charge of the military action there, the main reason being the strengthening of the ABiH in that area, which was of strategic interest. Therefore, there was a military action, a military operation. This military operation led by Rajic, who I will recall had left Kiseljak and had passed across Serb territory -- and who is conducting an operation mobilising several units, in real time, minute by minute, the Main Staff -- the officers on duty in the Main Staff were following what was happening on the ground. And, for example, did they learn, in real time, that two soldiers of units led by Rajic had been killed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, during these proceedings you were able to see the first report which arrived about 7.00 in the evening, so that was the first report that Ivica Rajic had sent since his arrival on the 22nd, that he had sent to the Main Staff to brief them on what was happening. Therefore, for more than 24 hours he did not contact anyone or communicate with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is important, what you have just said. You're saying under oath, and I insist, that in the case that I am quoting, the case of Stupni Do, there was no evaluation of the situation in real time by the duty officers in the Main Staff, and therefore by you, and you are telling us that you learnt about this at 1900 hours; that is, at 7.00 in the evening you learnt what had happened. But when you say that to me, General Petkovic, in military terms, is it normal functioning or should the military command not be constantly in contact with the military operations being conducted on the ground, or was this impossible in view of the situation at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, Ivica Rajic was not sent there to conduct any kind of operations. That is my first observation. And the Main Staff and the rest of us did not expect Ivica Rajic to conduct any kind of operations in that area. Ivica Rajic was sent there to stabilise the front-line which had been broken through by the ABiH from the village of Kopljari towards certain features which were closer and closer to the town of Vares. That was his only assignment. In view of such a situation, it was left up to Ivica Rajic to reconnoiter the situation, to report to us, report to his superiors in the chain of command. However, Ivica Rajic violated the rules regarding the duty to report, and for the whole day on the 22nd he did not report to anyone as to what he had done during that day, nor had he proposed actions for further approval. He carried out the operation in Stupni Do on his own initiative, which he was not assigned to do, and it was only in the evening that he sent a report on the events in Stupni Do. And we were all faced with a fait accompli. We didn't know what was happening in Stupni Do exactly, because even his report didn't give us a proper insight. Then additional reports were required by members of the Main Staff. And I, myself, on the 25th, asked for additional information as to what had happened in Stupni Do. So there was a certain interruption in the links between the operation and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, if what you are saying conforms with reality, and that is that Mr. Rajic had his principal mission to consolidate the front-line, that is why he was there, he wasn't there to conduct an offensive operation, fine. Why not? But in view of such a hypothesis, he arrives there and he finds that facing him he has ABiH units in large numbers - I have even seen a figure, 200 - and these units are firing at him, that he has dead and wounded, and that there is a real military problem, because it is no longer a question of consolidating the front, but he had to face up to a military action with casualties. And in view of such a situation, should not Rajic have, through the communication means he had at his disposal, immediately inform, and I underline "immediately," inform the commander of the operational zone so that: one, he should brief him on the situation; secondly, to request, if necessary, reinforcements? Would that not be the procedure that he should have followed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, that would be the procedure, but even I should add that that very evening he should have informed the staff of his decision, or, rather, to request approval or rejection. He didn't do either of those things. He didn't even go to Stupni Do. When he dismissed the persons who had come from the western part of the front-line together with Mr. Stosic, he made the decision to head for Stupni Do, and he did this early in the morning. And probably for those reasons, until he had completed what he had intended, he didn't wish to report to any institution. There was a dispute over a report sent on the -- at 11.00. He claimed that he hadn't done it. If it is in dispute, then the first report he sent was in the evening, around 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We shall look at document P551.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just comment on this document first, 9234? I don't know who prepared it, but the names of departments are not correctly indicated, nor the names of certain positions. For example, O, all the persons had the status of chiefs or heads, and here it says "Commander of the artillery." There's no commander of the artillery. There is the chief of the engineers, the chief of communications, et cetera. Here, it always says "Heads," and for the artillery it says "Commander," and he's not a commander of the artillery. Also, there are errors in the names of certain departments, but they are not so important. I think the most important mistake is that there is no such position as an artillery commander in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. There seems to be a problem of translation. Mr. Registrar, General Praljak tells us that he's having problems. No, it's working now. General Petkovic, with respect to the last document, which is a Prosecution document, you are telling us that there are errors. And you have indicated those errors, and it is in the transcript now. I'd like us to look at document P551 -- 151. 151, I'm sorry. We have the document in your own language, and that is most important. You can see it's a document dated the 8th of April, 1992, signed by Mr. Boban, regarding the creation of the Croatian Defence Council. What I am interested in, first of all, is the preamble, because the decision is motivated by a certain situation. And in the preamble that you can read, as I can, General Petkovic, it is indicated that there is an aggression and that there is a disintegration of the system of defence due to the impotence of the legal authorities of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which appears to be motivating Article 1 and 2, the formation of the HVO -- the military of the HVO. In April 1992, was that the situation that you, yourself, experienced; that is, there was no legal authority on the ground, it was absent, and you had to face an enemy? Was that, indeed, the situation or not, because this document is a document of the Prosecution and it says that Mr. Boban created the HVO in an illegal manner, in a certain sense, in order to carry out the project of the so-called joint criminal enterprise? That is the thesis of the OTP, through this document. But in this document, in the preamble there is reference to a particular situation. What would be your comment, please?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is quite understandable, because this date, the 8th of April, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, the accused cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me now? Yes. Your Honours, it is quite understandable that on this date, the 8th of April, 1992, the impotence of the legal authorities in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is reflected in the fact that Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have structured units which could at this point in time resist the aggression of the JNA and the VRS, which was the situation on the ground. In view of this, and at a time of fierce fighting at Kupres conducted by the HVO against the JNA and the VRS, Mr. Boban is conscious of the situation that the legal authorities in that area, or in the area of Herzegovina and even in the so-called free part of Bosnia, can still not establish significant military effectives [as interpreted], and he made the decision that the Croats should organise themselves as the Croatian Defence Council to represent a compact whole which would resist this aggression. This decision by Mate Boban fully corresponds to a later decision by Mr. Izetbegovic on the proclamation of a state of war, in which he says that the proclamation of a state of war is aimed at the right of the citizens, through individual and collective self-defence, to ensure the most effective use of the people in defence from aggression. So the people are entitled, individually and collectively, to defend themselves, their interests, and the interests of those living with them. Therefore, the Croatian people did have the right, if the area where they and others were living were at risk, to organise defence, and that is what he did. Already on the 4th of April, 1992, he was attacked, and he successfully resisted the JNA and the VRS throughout the territory of Kupres municipality and parts of the municipalities of Livno and Tomislavgrad. Therefore, Mr. Mate Boban took the decision at a time of the fiercest fighting in Kupres, when there were no government forces there at the time. And you heard when the commander of the army from Vakuf testified here, when I asked him about Kupres, he doesn't even remember what happened. And they were separated by a mountain chain, and from this he could have observed the entire Kupres Plateau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, Article 2 mentions the fact that the objectives shall be to defend the sovereignty of the territories of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and to protect the Croatian people, but this might seem important, what has also been added is "as well as other peoples." So when I read Article 2, I have the impression that this text has a very broad scope. The HVO --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honours. Mr. Mate Boban couldn't make the decision to expand this to incorporate the entire region of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, Mr. Mate Boban took this decision for a narrow area where he did wield influence and could establish units made up of the Croatian people and anybody else who wished to join. Mate Boban could not make a decision which would hold true for the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That kind of decision would be up to the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make, and it did gradually decide to establish its units and to have them involved in combat operations. Otherwise, I've already said that I arrived in Herzegovina -- or, rather, when I arrived in Herzegovina, I was surprised to see that the Presidency of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces should, in that part from the Prozor-Jablanica line towards the Croatian border, did not have any operative team or command on duty and no established unit, the strength of a brigade or anything else, except for the Independent Battalion in Mostar. Therefore, Mr. Izetbegovic quite obviously accepted the involvement of the Croatian Defence Council and Mr. Boban and everybody else, their involvement in the defence of that part of the territory, and he devoted himself to the establishment of units in other parts further into Bosnia-Herzegovina, in depth. And we can see this in his order at the end of May and beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, thank you for your answer, but your answer is very lengthy, very interesting. But you know that we have time restrictions. It's perhaps the fact that you have been familiar with Geneva diplomats, who allowed you to express yourself at length, I don't know. But try to be more brief, more concise, because that will allow me to follow up with a series of questions. Otherwise, I will have to limit myself because of time restrictions. However, if you believe that it's important to say some things, well, take your time. We'll have a look at P274.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P274 is a document of the 20th of June, 1992. It's from the president, Mr. Izetbegovic, and it concerns a proclamation of a state of war. This might help us understand the previous document that we had a look at. As you can see in this document, you have a preamble in which Mr. Izetbegovic explains the situation. There is an act of aggression, and 70 per cent of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is occupied, which means that only 30 per cent of the territory remains free. Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at item 2 of this decision, where the following is stated: "The proclamation of the state of war is based on individual and collective rights of citizens to self-defence ..." When I see this sentence, I wonder whether Mr. Izetbegovic considered that all citizens, Serbs, Croats, or Muslims, or any community in which there were Croats and Muslims, not Serbs, because the Serbs were the aggressors, should defend themselves. Is that what is stated?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is what is stated here, but I would include also the part of the Serbs who remained in these areas and put themselves at the service of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as Mr. Izetbegovic says. And ultimately the deputy Chief of the General Staff, Jovo Divjak, was a Serb, himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at item 3, where the armed forces - it's in the plural - are to take measures. We've already discussed the use of the plural. That is -- you're stating your position for the first time. It's perhaps useful to hear what you have to say. What does it mean? What does it mean when one says "the armed forces" and when this is put in the plural?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, "Mr. Izetbegovic" means all those forces, regardless of what their names are, who want to place themselves in a position whereby they would defend the free territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the Patriotic League that existed, the Territorial Defence that was under inception, the HVO, and everybody else, all the others who wished to oppose the aggression by Republika Srpska and the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you include the HVO in "the armed forces." Have a look at item 5, where it says that the UN Security Council is informed of this document. That's what it states.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina informed the United Nations about the aggression that had been launched against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean on the 20th of January, 1992 -- the 20th of June, correction, 1992, the international community, and the highest level of the international community, the Security Council, is aware of the fact that there's been an act of aggression by the Serbs and that the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, responding to the aggression, and the HVO forms part of these forces?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, Your Honours, because it was only the president of the Presidency who could say that an aggression had been carried out. Nobody could say that before him. So if on that day, he notes that an aggression had been conducted against Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he defined the aggressor, he informed the Security Council thereof, or, rather, the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a look at document P00279. The date is the 20th of June again, so the date is important. And you are the author of this document; is that correct? The 26th of June is the date. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you know that in the indictment and in the Prosecution's allegations, there's an international armed conflict that is mentioned and the intervention of the Croatian Army. Have a look at paragraph 2, "Operative and tactical situation." You, yourself, say that the HVO, with the assistance of the Croatian Army, with considerable assistance provided by the Croatian Army, well, that's what you meant, and what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours -- Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the forces of the Croatian Army acted in the border belt, because the forces of the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska were deployed both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. They were united forces, and along with an operation from the HVO to liberate the Neretva Valley, the Croatian Army forces in this border belt repelled the Serb forces and Army of Republika Srpska from the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and thus made a considerable contribution to liberating the territory east of the Neretva River on the day before the war was declared -- a state of war was declared in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3 in the English version - it's certainly page 3 in the version you have, too - you provide a list of the forces: 3.500 in Mostar, 3.400; Siroki Brijeg, 1.500, et cetera, so we have the strength of troops there. We can see that in the English version and in your version too. And below, you explain that, in fact, the HVO forces represent a division. So when you drafted this in June 1992, was that, in fact, the real situation with regard to HVO forces? There was barely one division?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, this is my proposal as to how the HVO forces could be reduced to this amount. The HVO forces, up until then, were far greater, and it was my assessment that given the present situation, the prevailing situation, that in the Neretva River Valley a reorganisation of forces should take place whereby these forces could be capable of controlling the area and defending it, and preventing any further attacks or repeated attacks by the Army of Republika Srpska and the JNA. So these are not the forces that were there. This is an assessment of how far we should reduce the forces in existence and also guarantee the security situation and defence lines reached at that point in time. So there were far larger forces before, and I think -- my thinking was, We've liberated the left bank of the Neretva River, we don't need that many forces now for us to be able to hold the line. So it was my proposal to assess how many soldiers we really did need to hold the line and provide security, and guarantee that the Serbs could not return to the Neretva. And all other HVO forces were in West Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, and so on and so forth. This is just a portion of those forces which were located south of Mostar, Mostar, and Stolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a look at the last document before the break. It's an important emblematic document. We've spoken about it often. It's been discussed in many cases before this Tribunal. P476. It is an incriminating document, a Prosecution document, and it's a decision from the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's a decision that everyone is very familiar with. Before we have a look at the contents of the document: This decision is dated the 18th of September, 1992. As far as you can remember, General Petkovic, when you were the chief of staff, at the front-line, in your office, on the roads, do you become familiar with the existence of the document at the time? Now, of course, you are familiar with it. But at the time, were you aware of this decision? Did you learn about this decision anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I never heard about this decision. And on the -- well, this is the 18th of September. So if we look at the date and we look at the 7th of October, when I was in Sarajevo and so on, nobody had the courage to say, Listen, Petkovic, when I occupied a high post, a month ago such and such a decision was taken and it's up to us to inform you about that. No, nobody showed me a decision of that kind with Izetbegovic, Halilovic, and Boban, and Mile Akmadzic, the prime minister. We were in Geneva. Nobody told us that the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina had made any decision. So this was hidden, and it was left to be used at an opportune moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the decision, item 5, we have a list of all the texts that are being annulled. Five refers to the Decree on the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was adopted on the 3rd of July, 1992. So that was a decree that was to be annulled. Can you see that? Is that what it states?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour, I can see that it was annulled. The Decree on the Armed Forces, which was passed on the 3rd of July, 1992, was annulled, but not the decision on the establishment of the HVO which we saw under P5115 [as interpreted], and the date of that was the 8th of April, 1992, because the Constitutional Court did not have the right to annul anybody -- any nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina the right to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina. They don't have the right to do that, because the Constitution says that he has the right, individually, and with others, to help to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I correct the transcript. On page 30, line 22, the general gave us the number of the document. It was P151.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that that document was not abolished and that the Constitutional Court did not have the right to annul the document. It can't deny Croats the right, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, because that is a constitutional category and provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that you have some legal knowledge, given your comments. It's not surprising, in view of the high-level position you had at the time. As you have some knowledge, you can certainly clarify a certain number of points for us. The Constitutional Court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which functioned in an almost identical way to the way in which constitutional courts function in other countries, in my country, for example, and because of that it's not surprising when I see this text - it's quite traditional, quite normal - you say that the Constitutional Court acted on its own initiative, that's what it says. As far as you know, could this Court seize itself, act on its own initiative?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says here that was the initiative of the Constitutional Court, itself, and that on the basis of this auto-initiative, that it took this decision and these decisions. Now, I interpret this in the following way: that the Constitutional Court did not consult anybody else. I don't know whether by law it was duty-bound to do so, but in my opinion it would have been a good idea if it had consulted the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina to see what should be done at that given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The decision doesn't have any page numbers, but I have a page number 0050-7515. On this page, the Constitutional Court explains the legal foundation for annulling the decree. It's paragraph 3 in the English version. It's not necessary to have a look at it. It's sufficient to look at me and to listen to me. It says that the territorial organisation and the political organisation of these municipalities, in order to make sure that it's in conformity with the Constitution, has to be implemented in accordance with the law, through a legislative procedure. And the text on the armed forces that are to be annulled wasn't adopted by law. That's what the Constitutional Court says. If this had been done legally, then they would have said it's quite legal. So that is the reason that resulted in this annulment. The legislative procedure that should have been followed wasn't followed. It's not excluded -- they don't exclude that had the procedure been followed, the HVO could be in accordance with the Constitution. As far as you know at the time, did the Parliament -- or could Parliament convene in order to have a certain text, a certain document, adopted legally?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not have been convened. At that time, neither Mr. Izetbegovic could leave Sarajevo, so he had to wait until July or later to leave Sarajevo for the first time, not to have delegates come to the Assembly. And which delegates? We're talking 1992 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's now time for our break. We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Judge Prandler apologises. He will not be present. He will join us as soon as possible. He has a medical reason for his absence, but he will join us as soon as possible. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Sorry for my absence this morning. I had something come up that I was not able to reschedule, but I appreciate the Court's indulgence. Your Honours, just while it's fresh in our mind, I wasn't sure -- I was reading the transcript of the first session and the ruling at the first about the re-examination, and it wasn't clear to the Prosecution - perhaps it's clear to others, perhaps not - the intention of the timing of the additional questions that the Petkovic Defence might be allowed to put. It was the impression -- it was the majority impression, if you will, on the Prosecution side that what was understood or what was intended was that following all of the Judges' questions, including yours, Mr. President, but once you'd completed, there would be an opportunity then for the Petkovic Defence to raise any questions arising out of your -- out of your questions, the Judges' questions, because at one point in one of the statements it said this would happen prior to the cross-examinations by the other parties. However, then toward the end of the ruling, it then talked about during the re-examination, and so it's not clear to the Prosecution, with all great respect, what the Chamber's thinking or intentions are, whether the Petkovic Defence would then seek to supplement its direct examination immediately following the Judges' questions or something else. We would appreciate any additional clarification, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, clearly the clarification of Your Honours' ruling is for Your Honours. I can simply tell you what the Petkovic Defence understanding was, and it really stems -- and it seems to us that it's just a supposed ambiguity has been found in what the Trial Chamber said, but we had understood that at page 2 of today's transcript, where Your Honour said: "The Chamber finds that regarding the subjects raised during the questions put by the Judges to Milivoj Petkovic at the end of the examination-in-chief and before the cross-examination by the other parties," Your Honours were simply referring to the point at which Your Honours' questions were being put, i.e., at the end of the examination-in-chief and before the cross-examination by the other parties. And we had certainly understood, from -- in fact, Your Honour, thank you. We regarded Your Honour's ruling this morning as very clear and helpful, but we had understood that the re-examination was going to include, of course, the normal questions arising out of cross-examination by the other parties and then any questions which arose out of Your Honour's questions to Mr. Petkovic. Clearly -- well, we're both inviting clarification, if there's any doubt at all, but that was our clear understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, may I just put the Petkovic Defence position. We are in the second half of the presentation of the Defence case now, and thus far, at least in three Defence teams, we had the situation whereby Judges ask questions during the examination-in-chief, and the reactions to the Judges' questions, all the Defence teams have had experience with this, and we also have experience from the examination of General Praljak, and never has the question arisen as to whether the Defence conducting the examination-in-chief has the right to ask a question following a Judge's question. It is quite clear that the Defence teams that are going to cross-examine will refer to the questions put by the Judges, because those questions are, indeed, relevant ones, and so far it's never been contested that the Defence team conducting the examination-in-chief has the same rights. So I'm just going to repeat what my colleague Mr. Stewart has already said, that your decision of this morning is quite logical and expected and quite in keeping with practice in this courtroom thus far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. I listened to the decision with quite a bit of alarm, and I even had a conversation with my client. I spoke with some of my colleagues. And here are the reasons why. And before, perhaps, I give the reasons, let me go back to what Mr. Mundis had once reminded us with respect to the way, in the past, at least, how trials were conducted. There would be direct, there would be cross-examination, Judges' questions, then there would be redirect, but also all of the parties would have an opportunity to ask questions concerning the Judges' questioning. Now, obviously things have moved on. This is a larger case. In this particular instance, Mr. President, I must say the way this trial is being conducted, at least right now, is rather unprecedented, in the sense that the Presiding Judge is asking questions like a party. The Rules were not designed in that fashion. However, I think an interpretation of the Statute certainly does not restrict a Judge to asking questions, and certainly it's not my position to restrict a Judge from conducting the examination that he or she feels is necessary in achieving the right result at the end of the case. However, having said that, what is being done right now, Your Honours, is you're conducting an additional direct examination, plus cross-examination, and that's fine. This is -- you know, Judges normally don't cross-examine, they examine, and a Judge can ask direct and leading questions back and forth. However, it puts the others at a grave disadvantage, because you go into an area -- you've restricted us to 36 minutes. Now I have to decide, Do I do what I was planning on doing? Do I challenge, or do I supplement any questions based on what the -- the party that did the direct examination? Do I address your questions? Today, there were several instances where I would have wanted follow-up questions. They did not come. Obviously, I cannot control the proceedings. But now I have to make some choices. So given the circumstances, it is highly prejudicial to the parties to just restrict us to the time that you've given us. That's number 1. Number 2, where I think it's fundamentally unfair. And I rarely use this word, but this is -- I think it's fundamentally unfair to suggest that the party who brings a witness can scratch an issue, then force the other party to maybe go into the issue, and then, on redirect, come back with all the ammunition that was available. And I indicated it's called "sand-bagging," that's the terminology that we're using. Now, why is that fundamentally unfair? Because in this procedure we do not have the opportunity for re-cross-examination, and so there is a reason why I think Judge May insisted on the British rule of putting your case to the witness. You have to do it at the time. And so I think many of my colleagues are very, very concerned that what's going to happen is now you've gone into areas that the Petkovic Defence did not go into, and so now the Petkovic Defence obviously, and rightfully, can go into those areas on redirect -- on redirect examination, introduce documents, thus depriving the rest of us, albeit not intentionally, or maybe intentionally - I don't know, it doesn't matter - but depriving the rest of us from then responding. We certainly -- you know, so have you to look at it from that standpoint. The Rules are designed so that everybody has a fair opportunity to be heard, even under the time constraints, and so I think that we need to think about this. I'm not asking for any particular measures right now. I don't know what Mr. Scott and his team feel. I didn't mention the -- bring up the issue with them. But we are concerned that we don't have enough time. My client believes that right now we need about two hours. Now, maybe that's unrealistic. Maybe that's asking for too much. I don't know. But certainly you're going to do a three- or four-day direct examination, on top of six hours -- six actual hours of direct examination by the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this does directly concern the Petkovic Defence, which is why I'm on my feet again. Mr. Karnavas raises two separate points, and he went back to his first point at the end. His first point is simply the question of time. I've got nothing to say about that right now, except that if at some appropriate point in the course of the examination of Mr. Petkovic any of the parties believe that they have a justified case to apply for more time, they can make that application. We can cross that bridge when we come to it, and they can make the application. I've got nothing to say about it until any such application is specifically made. So far as his second point is concerned, scratching an issue, not bringing something up in examination-in-chief, Your Honour, this has been dealt with. This has been debated, it has been discussed and argued, it has been ruled upon. It's effectively been ruled upon in Your Honour's clear ruling this morning. I don't know whether Mr. Karnavas wasn't here on some of the dates when it was debated, and I don't mean that in any way offensively. I just don't know whether he was. But the fact is that that issue has been resolved. He's raising it all over again, when it's already been decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I might be allowed to follow on, since we're dealing with the Petkovic Defence. I apologise to my colleague. Your Honours, just let me add one more element. I fully support everything that Mr. Karnavas said before me about the fear, on the part of certain Defences, as to what can happen during examination by the Judges, and that they won't have enough time to react during the cross-examination; and, on the other hand, that we, as Defence counsel for General Petkovic, will have time to react to what the Judges raise through their questions and signify it as an important area. So I completely agree with Mr. Karnavas, and I do consider that it is a matter that must be resolved, and that all Defence teams must have the feeling that they are being given enough time to go about their business in the right way, as they see fit. That is why I fully support the reassertion of the institution of a re-cross-examination. But let me say that as far as I know, Your Honours, nobody was ever forbidden from examining in re-cross-examination if they so desired and requested. And let me just remind you that I did make this request when it came to a Prosecution witness, Marijan Biskic, after the cross-examination by the Coric Defence, and similarly I also requested this for a Defence witness, Bruno Stojic, for Mr. Ivan Bandic, after the Prosecutor's cross-examination. And I explained to Your Honours why I wished to recross examine, and I was given the right to do so. So I consider that my colleagues now, once we're examining General Petkovic, must have the right for re-cross-examination and must know that they enjoy that right, if they see fit and if the need arises for that. And there's no doubt that the Trial Chamber will permit them to re-cross-examine, if they should so request.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, and I will endeavour to be brief. In my submission, I have a lot of sympathy for the position put forward by the Prosecution. There's no question at all about the right of the Defence for General Petkovic to ask questions arising out of the questions put forward by the Bench. It's simply a question of timing. Whether or not that is called re-examination, or whether or not Your Honours simply give leave to ask additional questions, is an issue of nomenclature. Nothing turns upon it at all. But it does, in my respectful submission, lend to judicial efficiency to actually have questions put by the Defence for General Petkovic immediately after the Bench has asked questions that they think are necessary. The reason for that is to avoid confusion. Down the line, when we come to the issue of re-examination proper, and of course the Rules, I think it's fair to say, when they were initially adopted, in large measure initially from the American Bar Association Rules, contemplated a common-law adversarial system, but this of course is not a purely adversarial, common-law system, it is a hybrid of both, and I have no qualms at all regarding questioning from the Bench. Indeed, it is to be welcomed in large measure. But, Your Honours, when one is looking at a partage of process, the idea of re-examination, in large measure, is to allow the Defence or the party putting questions to have the final word to clarify issues so that nothing is left ambiguous. Now, Your Honours, if we can draw a distinction between questions from the Bench, who, of course, are not a party, it may, indeed, lend clarity. So what I do, in my respectful submission, put forward is that after, Mr. President, you have finished your questions, and after any questions from other members of the Bench in this nature, an opportunity is given to the Defence for General Petkovic to ask questions arising out of the questions from the Bench. Once that is done, all parties will have a clearer picture as to the issues that General Petkovic wishes to put forward, and we can resume with normal cross-examination. And at the end of that, issues that arise out of cross-examination from the parties can be put by General Petkovic. That way, there's no confusion with the Defence for any of us, or the Prosecution, jumping up and saying, Your Honours, this doesn't arise out of cross-examination from the parties, because nobody can take cover with the general rubric that, no, it doesn't arise out of cross-examination from the parties, but it arises out of questioning from the Bench. I think that, in essence, is the nub of my submission, in support of the Prosecution, that any additional questions arising out of Your Honours' questions from the Bench should be done immediately after the questions have been put and prior to

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we can help by saying that, actually, on this --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I got up first. So as a lady, may I be given priority?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You can have priority certainly for that reason, of course; not one I would have suggested, myself, but because you did stand up first. I just didn't see you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, sometimes have you to resort to all possible means available. I'd just like to add to what my colleagues have already said, Mr. Karnavas and the rest, Mr. Khan, and tell you of the problems I faced with two practical examples. Yesterday, when the Trial Chamber divided up the time to the Defence teams, it had in mind summary and direct examination by the Petkovic Defence, or in-chief by the Petkovic Defence. There was no indication, for example, that a lot would be discussed about the military police, and in that way the Coric Defence was given 36 minutes, pursuant to the Trial Chamber's ruling. Yesterday, however, we spent a whole session discussing -- or, rather, Judge Antonetti examined Mr. Petkovic on the topic of the military police, and they were broad topics linked to the military police; what the establishment of the military police was, its structure, the chain of command, and so on. Now, for each of those topics, for the general to be shown documents and for him to be given enough time to read them, if we take it that we need five minutes per document, then in 30 minutes we can only deal with six documents. That's the math of it. So that's the question of time. And I think that after the Judges' questions, we should re-think the time allotted to the parties. The second question that arises, and that's where I wish to support Mr. Khan in what he said, linked to timing; that is to say, when the Petkovic Defence, in our opinion, should conduct its additional examination. From the documents, we can see that Judge Antonetti, in his examination -- and that was broached in chief, the topic of prisons and forced labour. Now, what we have heard on those two subjects thus far from General Petkovic is only this: that the Main Staff -- or, rather, that he had nothing to do with that. Now, at this point in time, perhaps I've got something wrong, but he just dealt with the role of the Main Staff and didn't deal with the roles of the other accused in these proceedings. But what can happen is that during these additional questions, for example, and after the Judges' questions, following the Judges' questions, we hear something quite new, new additional information, because of which we would need to cross-examine again, and then what will happen is that we will be in this vicious circle. We'll have cross-examination, then we'll have re-examination or redirect, then perhaps some of us will ask the right to re-cross-examine, and then the Petkovic Defence, who certainly has the right to do so, have another re-examination session, and I see no end to it. And that's why I think it would be far more practical and far more proper to -- and fairer to all the parties concerned that the Petkovic Defence conduct its additional questions and asks its additional questions before cross-examination, that is to say, additional questions following the Judges' questions, so that we can again re-think the time allotted to all the rest who are going to cross-examine. So that is my proposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic -- wait a moment, please. I have a question to put to General Petkovic, and everything will depend on his answer. General Petkovic, you have listened to the debate. I should like to know whether you want me to ask you questions or not. If you say, No, I will stop asking you questions. But if you tell me, Yes, ask me questions, I will continue with my questions. Why? Because when General Praljak was in your seat, he told us, I wish to answer all questions. I'm here for the establishment of the truth. And it is under those conditions that I put questions to him. So if, like General Praljak, you wish the truth to be established, if you want me to ask you questions, you tell me; if not, I will stop, and I will give the floor immediately to Mr. Karnavas for the cross-examination. Everything depends on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I'm asking General Petkovic a question. Let him answer, and then afterwards I will give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I didn't appreciate it was specifically a question. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is a question addressed to Mr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall act no differently than General Praljak acted. So, yes, I will listen to all your questions and provide the answers. Whether you want those answers or not, I will give you the answers as I feel should be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you're not answering my question. Do you want me to ask you questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, I do. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To answer first to the counsel for Mr. Coric, it is true that I have touched questions relating to the military police. Mr. Stewart is going to have the floor, but it is I who has priority for the moment. I will give you the floor, Mr. Stewart, but let me respond to the counsel for Mr. Coric. Questions of the military police were addressed yesterday, but I did not insist on those questions. I just simply asked General Petkovic that he tell me how he imagined the relationships with the military police. He answered. I did not dwell on those issues and go into them in depth because I know that Mr. Coric has 50 hours in the future. He also has time allotted to him for the cross-examination, and after that he will have 16 hours for his case, and my understanding was that he would be testifying. So the questions of the military police will be examined at great length, and that is why I did not insist -- dwell on them. Secondly, to respond to Mr. Karnavas regarding the question of the Rules: The Rules envisage that there is the presentation of evidence by the Prosecution, then by the Defence for this witness, but the Rules also say that the Judges may decide as they wish in accordance with due process, and the Judges are allowed to pose questions at any time. And this has been said and re-said and confirmed by the Appeals Chamber. And it's efficient to refer to some decisions of the Appeals Chamber. It was astonished on several occasions that the Judges were not allowed to ask appropriate questions. Therefore, this emanates from the Rules. As excellently explained by Mr. Khan, we are in a hybrid system which is a combination of the two systems. The question put by Mr. Scott is important, and that is: At what point additional questions may be put. In the decision that I rendered in his absence, the following was stated, and I will repeat: The Chamber finds that regarding the subjects raised during the questions by the Judges put to Milivoj Petkovic at the end of the examination-in-chief and before the cross-examination, before the cross-examination, they may, upon authorisation of the Chamber, be raised by the Petkovic Defence during the additional examination. Therefore, the Chamber envisaged the possibility for Ms. Alaburic to intervene after me regarding additional questions emanating from my questions. That is what is stated in the decision. But she has to ask for this, because it is stated "upon permission of the Chamber." Therefore, at the end, she may say, You have raised in your questions points A, B, C, D, which I did not cover in the examination-in-chief. May I be allowed to ask some additional questions? The reply of the Chamber will be: Yes/No. If, Yes, then you will proceed with your questions. If, No, it will be afterwards. So I think it was clear. I don't see where the problem is. Mr. Stewart, I apologise for interrupting. You wanted to say something. Please proceed. I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Absolutely no apology necessary. In English, we sometimes say, "age before beauty," as between Mr. Coric's counsel and me, we went the other way around on this particular occasion. Your Honour, in fact in a sense, you've anticipated or pre-empted what we were going to say, because the Petkovic Defence was going to say whatever was intended by the initial ruling this morning, we had no strong position on whether questions arising out of Your Honours' questions should come before or after the cross-examination by the other parties. But Your Honour's just given a clear indication on that, anyway, and resolved what apparently was a slight ambiguity earlier today. But we would just then like to make two points. First of all, the question of whether any such further examination by Mr. Petkovic's own counsel, at the conclusion of Your Honours' questions, justifies or will justify any additional time for examination by any of the other parties, and particularly by the Prosecution, is an issue on which we do not accept that it will. Again, any such application would need to be made specifically and justified by the specific circumstances, but there should be no automatic adjustment. And that really is a corollary of what must be recognised and was implicitly recognised in one of my colleague's submissions a few minutes ago in relation to Judges' questions, which is that Judges' questions are not really easily categorised as examination-in-chief or cross-examination. They may be some sort of mixture or combination of any sort of questions, so that whether they do fairly then give rise to any justification for further time is an issue to be looked at very specifically in the specific circumstances.
