The only other point I'd make very briefly, Your Honour, is this: that, yes, we did note, of course, the qualification that further questions by the Petkovic Defence of our own client arising out of Your Honours' questions were to be with the permission of the Trial Chamber, but we would like to say this, not aggressively but very firmly, Your Honour, that it must only be in a pretty rare situation where the Trial Chamber had come to the conclusion that really nothing relevant could arise out of particular questions which have been raised by the Judges in the light of the answers that the opportunity of following up the Judges' questions should be denied, because it would be and is, in practical terms, inherently unfair for the Judges to raise an issue with the witness in this way and then not give us an opportunity of exploring that issue. And I will say, Your Honour, every Trial Chamber -- and really every Trial Chamber in this institution does adopt its own procedures, that's clear, and adapts the Rules as it thinks fit, but the Krajisnik trial hasn't been mentioned for a long time, and the last few times it was mentioned, not by me, although I lived it for two or three years. In the Krajisnik trial, we were always absolutely routinely, without any question whatever, given the right to follow up any Judges' questions, and that's actually what I'm familiar with in England, as it happens. I didn't welcome every single way in which the trial was conducted in the Krajisnik case. No counsel ever does. But that particular aspect of the trial was absolutely standard and does reflect, what is, as I've submitted, inherently fair. So we earnestly hope that we shall not be refused a reasonable opportunity and time to follow up any issues which we consider material raised by Your Honours in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Out of principle, Mr. President, I feel that I am compelled to clarify the record, because I don't want there to be any misunderstanding by you, or anyone else reading this record further down the line. I have never, ever stated that a Judge is not entitled to ask questions. What I have said is that the manner in which this trial is being presented is unprecedented. I know of no other case where a Judge does what you're doing. I'm not suggesting that you're not entitled to, but because you are acting as a party, as it were, it does pose some problems, some technical problems, because now we're under some time constraints. And we, who have to follow your questioning, who are bound by certain time constraints, may be prejudiced, because we will need more time to go into certain areas. So I just want to make it very clear that I never, ever stated that you could not ask questions, and that somehow, thanks to Mr. Khan, we all realise that this is a hybrid tribunal. We've all known this for some time, so I want to make this very, very clear. Number 2, I have state in the past that we're not here to get to the truth. It would be nice to get to the truth, but we're not here to get to the truth. That is not in the Statute. I want to be very, very clear on that. Mr. Praljak may want to get at the truth. That's his wish, and he's entitled to that. But the Rules claim and call for the Prosecution to meet its burden of proof. There lies the conundrum. It is not for the Judge to try to reach to the truth, because in doing so there is a blurring of the lines. The responsibility is on the Prosecution. They put the case together; they have that burden. They have a big team; they know what they're doing. But if the Judge is going to be seeking for the truth, and if that is your intention, Your Honour, we need to know clearly, because this is a matter that I would like interlocutory appellate review of, if we have changed the standard of proof and changed the burden of proof, because this is a case where the burden of proof lies on the Prosecution. The Judges are entitled to ask questions. I think the system was designed for the Judges to ask questions of clarification, but the system is also rather unclear. The Statute doesn't say where are the limitations. So recognising that, I fully agree that you're entitled to conduct your examination as you're doing, irrespective of the wishes of the accused who's decided to take the stand. Whether he wishes you to ask questions or not is irrelevant. He's here to answer questions, he wants questions, he's inviting you to ask questions. But I think that we cannot stray away from the Statute. Otherwise, we don't know what we're doing. We're left with a great deal of uncertainty. And I don't know if Mr. Scott wishes to be heard, but that's my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and I've been sitting patiently, and I think the Petkovic Defence has been up six or seven times now to my one. I guess I kicked this off with what I thought was a very straightforward question, a clarification, and it seems that other parties, in fact -- in fact, as it turns out, had a similar question. I do want to start my comments, Your Honour, my brief responses, to -- I've noticed the last few times that the Prosecution has gotten to its feet and raised a concern or asked a question, it seems to come back -- it seems to come back from the Petkovic Defence that somehow the Prosecution has something underhanded in mind, that there's something tricky going on, and I don't really appreciate being hit --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just don't know where Mr. Scott hears that, I really don't, but I can withdraw any suggestion of any trickiness. I'm amazed that anything I said should be understood that way, but I can assure Mr. Scott we never suggest, implicitly or expressly, anything underhand or tricky. And I've said a long time ago in this trial that it's part of my tradition, if ever I do, which I think is extremely unlikely -- if ever I find myself in a position where I felt that I should make any such suggestion that the Prosecution have been underhanded or tricky, or anybody had done that, I would say so in unequivocal, express terms so that they had the fairest opportunity to answer it. This is not the first time. It's one of many occasions on which Mr. Scott seems to hear me having -- suggesting something underhand, something tricky, something unprofessional. I do not do that, I have not done it. There's no such implication at all in anything I have said today, or, in fact, ever in this trial, in relation to Mr. Scott and his team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps, for starters, Your Honour, it would be a first step if counsel would not interrupt me during my --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Hardly complain that an interruption to withdraw what he has heard as an allegation of trickiness, so I don't apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Second interruption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are lost, because you've been going very fast, and it was very difficult to follow. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take on board Mr. Stewart's comments. I am being honest in saying that's how it's perceived by the Prosecution. We get up and we make what we think is a reasonable, good-faith request for clarification or a procedural point, and at least it feels to us -- let me put it that way. It feels to us that whenever we get up, that somehow it gets twisted into something tricky or underhanded, that we have something up our sleeve, and I'll say it again, we don't appreciate that. Now, having said that, I think this takes us right back to the questions that came up last week, and I was also on my feet at that time. And unfortunately Judge Trechsel, I think, wasn't here when we had the initial discussion on this point. It takes us right back to this central and fundamental point, and I do think, Your Honours, and I would ask the Chamber -- all the Judges to take on board, I think, the fact that you've had virtually almost -- not entirely, but almost all the Defence teams and the Prosecution on their feet, I hope the Chamber will take on board I think that's some indication of the seriousness of the issue that's being raised. This is a fundamental fairness question. It goes to the heart of the process. And what Mr. Karnavas says is right, this is a hybrid procedure. But in adopting hybrid procedures, there are impacts and consequences that may not arise out of any one given system, and I agree that when we have extensive questions by the Judges, and I don't question at all the Judges' right to do that, but it does expand the overall scope of the questions and the testimony substantially, and it does put things in a different procedural posture. So I ask the Chamber, all the Judges, take on board the fact that Mr. Karnavas, the fact that Mr. Khan, the fact that Mr. Coric's counsel, all of us are on our feet, I think, raises a legitimate and important concern. And, frankly, again with great respect, it's not up to the choice of Mr. Petkovic's Defence, whether they want to go now or they want to go later. It's not their choice. It's not their choice, with due respect. It's a matter of fairness. And if they decide to put it off and, Well, we choose to go to the end, well, we're right back to where we were. We have the fundamental unfairness of everyone saying -- Mr. Karnavas says being sand-bagged, or, in other words, being ambushed at the end of the day, when everyone else has to sit down, and then here it all comes. The process -- all the process is fundamentally against that, Your Honours. I think that, Your Honour, there has to be a fundamental assessment of the procedure and the process that we followed, and when the sequence should be given. And I do believe, and I do submit, especially after having heard the submissions over the last few minutes, I think it would be entirely fair and entirely appropriate, in this hybrid system of ours, for the Petkovic Defence to ask -- have additional direct examination following the completion of the Judges' questions, and then -- only then can both the co-accused and the Prosecution -- and I'll say it again, maybe no one believes it, but I tend to believe, and I will always believe that the Prosecution is entitled to a fair trial too. After that, then the co-accused and the Prosecution will be in a position to conduct their further examinations. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has rendered a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, just one sentence. I'd just like to say the following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, first I'll respond to Mr. Scott, and then I'll give you the floor. I wanted to tell Mr. Scott that when he raised this issue, the Chamber's oral decision dealt with the issue. After the end of the examination, you should ask -- not for the authorisation to put additional questions. Naturally, if you need time, the Chamber will deliberate about that. If you need additional time to deal with Mr. Scott's preoccupations, well, naturally you'll have the same time as the time that you used. So that's it. What's important is that we know what Mr. Petkovic has to say with regard to his position as the chief of staff and with regard to the documents, because in a few months' time the Chamber will have deliberated about the allegations in the indictment, and we'll have to decide about all these matters. Now, as far as the demonstration of truth is concerned, I'd like to remind you that in the Rules -- I don't have the Rules in front of me, but in the Rules it says that the Judges control -- or have control over the questions put to make sure that no time is wasted and in order to determine the truth. That is what is stated in the Rules. The Judges also have the obligation to ensure that the truth is determined. I didn't invent this. That's what's stated in the Rules, and I apply the Rules, as does everyone else. So, Ms. Alaburic, I interrupted you because I wanted to respond to Mr. Scott. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I do apologise. I wasn't aware of the fact that I was, in fact, interrupting you. I wanted to express the Petkovic Defence's position. We have absolutely nothing against us asking additional questions with regard to the questions put by the Judges prior to questions being put by the other Defence teams and the Prosecution. That's not a problem for us. If that's your decision, we will abide by the decision. At this point in time, I believe that we have another three additional questions that shouldn't take up more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have another three questions that should take up 10 minutes. We've spent 30 minutes now on these issues. General Petkovic, what I wanted to say was that when I put questions to you on the basis of certain documents, I always take into account the fact that I have to allow the other parties to come back and deal with the response. It's in their interest. For example, when I asked you, When did you meet Mr. Prlic, what was your impression of him, did he say anything about a Greater Croatia, et cetera, you answered that question, and now, in the light of that, if Mr. Karnavas is interested in the matter, he can go back to the subject, and the Prosecution can similarly return to the subject when putting questions to you. I always put questions in a manner that allows everyone to return to the subject. That has always been the way I proceeded. And there are certain cases, however, when Judges say, Once I've put my questions, no other party can intervene. I act in a contrary manner. That is why I preferred to put questions after you. I could have waited for everyone to express themselves, and then at the very end I could have put 10 questions to you to put things back into order. That's not how I proceed. All my questions are open questions, as you have noticed. As I noticed that you were at the front-line, well, if you say, I don't want to answer a question, I don't see why I should force you to answer a question. I am here to put questions to you so that we can examine the documents together, the charges against you, to examine your testimony as well. That's interesting. The burden of proof is on the Prosecution. No one questions that. But perhaps you have a point of view that relates to the Prosecution's claims, and that is what I'm interested in. I'll now move on to the following document, which is P00827. Very well. You can see the document. Your name appears in the document. That's why I'm using it. Otherwise, I don't see why it would be of interest. And the subject has been dealt with, in addition, in the course of the examination-in-chief, because there was a meeting in Sarajevo between you and Mr. Mladic. So that's the reason for using this document. General Morillon sent this document to Zagreb, and it's on the summaries of interviews that took place in Sarajevo. General Petkovic, have you seen this document before? Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at 5(a). That's what I'm interested in. In a discussion with Karadzic, Karadzic said the following: He reaffirmed the rights of all Croats and Muslims to freedom in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to security, and to self-determination. Mr. Karadzic reaffirmed the rights of all Serbs, Croats and Muslims. When I saw this, I asked myself if -- when you met with all the participants at the conference, to the best of your recollection, did Mr. Karadzic recognise that the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims should live in freedom in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me answer, before that, that I didn't attend the meeting with Karadzic. This is a meeting that was initiated for the four parties to meet and discuss certain problems in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those were the Croats in Bosnia, the Serbs in Bosnia, the Muslims in Bosnia, and for the Republic of Croatia to join in, and this was the beginning of individual encounters prior to such a four-partite meeting. I did not attend this meeting, but at the end, on the 20-something -- 29th, I discussed -- I talked to General Mladic with General Morillon, and before that he talked to General Bobetko and made some conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall now move on to the next document, P00831. I should like you to look at the first page of the document. You see, when asking questions, I do my homework, and I'll tell you why. You see this document. It is indicated "New York," and -- it is destined for New York, and it says "For information for Vance," you see, and it comes from UNPROFOR in Zagreb. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could the document please be displayed also in English. I don't see it, and I haven't gotten the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is there in English, too, on the left. This is just the first page. This is the first page. We'll see the document later. General Petkovic, I may cross my fingers and then not ask you -- or fold my arms and not ask you anything, but then I wouldn't know whether Mr. Vance had a complete insight into the situation. And when I see this document, I read it, and I say to myself, I have to ask a question, particularly of someone who went to Geneva. That is how I do my work. Perhaps others would prefer me to keep quiet, but I do the work for which I'm paid, even if it displeases everyone. General Petkovic, the subject is a meeting between Mladic and yourself, and I see that Mr. Vance is the addressee regarding information about the subject of your meeting. General Petkovic, according to your own feelings, in Geneva were they fully informed about everything that was happening in real time on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, they were informed about everything, and these meetings were meant to be preparatory meetings before going to the Geneva talks scheduled for January 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're telling me that Mr. Vance and all those with him, Lord Owen and the others, knew in real time what was happening on the ground, because this document leads us to assume that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Antonetti, Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, in addition to going to Sarajevo for these talks, they were constantly receiving reports from the UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia and Herzegovina; that is, General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us look at the document now. Look at page 2, and you will see small 3, which refers to you. Here we are. You see "3." That is you, General Petkovic. You're making proposals which are known, for Mr. Vance, because he was informed about them. And you're saying that a cease-fire is necessary, that the localities of Stolac, Mostar, Konjic, Travnik, Maglaj and Gradacac, should cease to be showed, the withdraw of heavy weapons should be carried out under UNPROFOR control, there should be freedom of movement along vital corridors, and the establishment of a hotline to resolve all incidents by negotiation. And then that there should be no movement or reinforcement of units, that prisoners, and bodies should be exchanged. You make all these proposals. Did you, indeed, make those proposals?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did make this proposal at a meeting held between me, Mladic, and General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look now, because we are going to go on to the next document, look at 4(b), "Additional Requests," not for additional time, but additional requests. There's reference to an agreement between Tudjman and Izetbegovic. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. General Mladic requested that the agreement or statement by President Tudjman and President Izetbegovic should be withdrawn regarding co-ordinated action against the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The document that was drafted by General Morillon, does it reflect well the climate at the time? Because we are talking about the end of November 1992, there were the events of Prozor, let me remind you. Does this document reflect the climate at the time, and the condition of the negotiations and the proposals made accurately?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this document does reflect the relation, and it relates to relations between the Serbs and the Croats. When I'm asking for the Serbs to stop shelling of Stolac, Mostar, Konjic, Gradacac, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, regarding the questions which will have to be addressed by the Judges when we deliberate, this issue was not raised. And I have a small sentence by General Mladic which is under item 4 and after your proposals, when General Mladic takes the floor. You see it? And this is what he says at the end: The difficulty, according to him, was that there were the forces of the Presidency with the HVO, and he says that the forces of the Presidency were mixed. Does that mean that General Mladic considered that he had facing him an army consisting of two components, HVO and ABiH, because apparently that is your "enemy," in quotation marks, that is speaking, so he certainly knows what he's speaking about? How would you interpret that phrase which I'm referring to now? And that is why am asking you this question, and I wish to be useful.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did ask for this, and he asked, Who is responsible for which part of the territory, and where there is joint responsibility by the - let us call them - allies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you knew General Mladic. I have never seen him. I have heard reference to him in the media. But you have met him, and you were in contact with him. When I see that General Morillon, who is somebody -- I don't know, and I have never seen him, again I have heard reference to him in the press, as everyone - when I see that he attributed to General Mladic the expression "Presidency forces," General Morillon and General Mladic are using this term, "Presidency forces," instead of talking "Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," or, "ABiH," or, "HVO." Why, in your view, are they saying "Presidency forces"? What does this mean, and what did it mean for Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic is saying this because he believes that all the forces there are under the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or under the control of President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may make a small correction. Page 61, line 22, the answer is registered as if it was Judge Antonetti speaking, but it was, in fact, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, for you, General Mladic believed that the armed forces of the Presidency were the HVO and the ABiH. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how far he went. In that sense, he called those forces "Presidency forces," but sometimes he would say, Define for me how far it is the BiH, how far the HVO, and how far you are together, so that he would know how to position himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, as you're someone who has met General Mladic, it may be -- it was useful to put this question to you, as no one else referred to it. P01139, that is the next question, the question of the ultimatum of the 15th of January, 1993. It is what is alleged by the Prosecutor, and he has the burden of proof. And regardless of that, we have a document here which is signed by you, yourself. I see, under A, you're saying all units of the HVO armed forces and of the ABiH in Provinces 3, 8, and 10 be placed under the command of the HVO, and then you address Provinces 1, 5, 9. I will not go into the details of this document, because this document has already been addressed. My question is a very simple one, General Petkovic. Is this document an ultimatum telling the ABiH that, From now on in Provinces 3, 8, and 10, it is us who will be in command; in others, it will be you? What did you envisage, writing this document? And this is an incriminating document.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I not consider this document to be any kind of ultimatum. This document was compiled in the conviction that in Zagreb, a political agreement had been reached between the two parties, and we acted in accordance with that document. In this document, it is not stated anywhere that the brigades of the ABiH or the HVO, who are domicile and who are in their own territory, have to leave that territory. If you read paragraph 4 or item 4, it says: "Members and units of the HVO armed forces and of the BH Army who do not submit to the commands in items 1 and 2 herein must leave the provinces where they do not belong." Which are the forces that do not belong, for instance, to the Mostar province? It could be a force brought by the HVO from Western Herzegovina. But all HVO forces of the operative zone and all the forces of the 4th Corps belong to the Mostar province, and no one is asking them to be removed, and there's no reason to do so. It is a reference to the provinces that do not belong. And all the forces of the 4th Corps and the Mostar Operative Zone do belong to Province -- I don't remember which number it was. Was it number 10, the Mostar province? But if we take the Black Swans, commanded by Zuka, who came from Igman or Sarajevo, they do not belong to that province. And, as such, they should be either re-subordinated, according to this document, or leave the province. Similarly, if the HVO has a company by Bruno Busic based in Mostar, but which may be in Central Bosnia, then it does not belong to Central Bosnia, and it, too, should either agree to be placed under command or simply leave it and go back to its domicile, and that is the area of Mostar, shall we say. Therefore, the local units, the domicile units, are both units of the ABiH and the HVO units formed in those municipalities and in those provinces. All others who happen to be there and do not belong to those provinces, if they do not agree to being re-subordinated to one or other party, they have to leave the province. No one is removing units that were formed out of people belonging to that province, and that is the heart of item 4. Then, also, the commands are invited to have talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when there's a document, there's always an explanation for a document, especially if it's a military order. The explanation here is one that has to be looked for in the preamble. So you can see, General Petkovic, I can just fold my arms and wait for the end of the judgement to say the criminal enterprise was, in fact, in place because the document says that in Provinces 3, 8 and 10, there was an ultimatum according to which the ABiH units should be subordinated to the HVO, and that would be the end of the story. But for me, a document is something that has to be looked at. And when, in the document -- when the document contains certain things that make me wonder, I have to put certain questions to myself, without interfering with the Prosecution or the Defence. So this is why I ask you to have a careful look at the preamble. Why is a reference made to agreements reached at the Geneva conference? Why is there such a reference here; for aesthetic reasons, or was there a real need felt to make such a reference here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on agreements reached in Geneva, and the agreement between the Croats and the Muslims, it was stated that the Croats and the Muslims should regulate their relations in Provinces 8, 10, and -- or, rather, 5 and 9 - I'm not quite sure - that they should resolve their relations on the basis of an agreement; that is to say, that they should sit down and state that in such and such a province, the situation would be such. And in medical [as interpreted] terms, it says that the HVO has Province 3, which is Posavina, no problem there; that the BH Army has the province - I think it was the Bihac province - no problems there; and that the Serbs must withdraw from all other territories and return to their provinces. Now, the BH Army and the HVO must sit down and find a common language for the situations in provinces where they are mixed, where the population is mixed. So that is the essence of the problems reflecting the military part and relations between the HVO and BH Army, in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Perhaps in Mr. Scott's cross-examination, he will return to this document. But, General Petkovic, you remember when Mr. Okun came and he spoke here at length?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You do. I understood, on the basis of what Mr. Okun said, but also on the basis of what the American ambassador who was in Zagreb said, I understood that the HVO, according to them, allegedly had, and I say "allegedly had" because I don't know the answer, allegedly had the intention of implementing the Geneva conclusions in advance, although not everything had been settled, not everything had been dealt with, and as a result we have this document. So what is your opinion of that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Geneva ultimately was never signed, because the third party didn't put its signature to the document. But without a doubt, Lord Owen and his team made every effort to have its project implemented between the Croats and the Muslims, and that's why he went to Zagreb, that's why he went to Medjugorje, and that's why he encouraged the Croats and Muslims to start with the implementation of that part which could be implemented, which meant the establishment of authority in the provinces and resolving the problem in the command of military units located in these joint provinces. And without any doubt at all, Lord Owen had several meetings with the delegate -- Croatian and Bosniak delegations to help him out and to help this process take effect, because he found that there were no significant problems between the Muslims and the Croats, and that then he could exert greater pressure on the Serb side, if they agreed. So that is why there were frequent meetings outside Geneva between the Croats and the Muslims attended by Lord Owen and his team, to encourage the Croats and Muslims to start with implementing the agreement, regardless of the fact that the third party, the Serbs, had not actually signed yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The following document, which doesn't have the same importance, but a minor secondary question, P01118. It's a document from General Morillon addressed to Mr. Mate Boban. And it refers to Kordic, too. It says "Colonel." It's following the death of a British soldier in Gornji Vakuf that the general, General Morillon, asked Mr. Mate Boban to investigate the matter, et cetera. This drama, this misfortune, because a soldier was killed, was this an event that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, because our people in Vakuf composed a report linked to this particular incident, and they had to inform Mr. Boban about it so that he had our version of events, although the event actually occurred at a point in time when, in Gornji Vakuf, there was a meeting between the missions of the BH Army, the HVO, and the commander of SpaBat, Mr. Stewart. So at the time they entered the command, the headquarters, for that meeting, that's when this British soldier was killed in front of Hotel Radusa on Marsal Tito Street in Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a look at the following document, P1322. It's a document we've already seen. You are the author of the document. That's why I'm showing it to you. And it's in relation to an agreement between Boban and Izetbegovic reached in Geneva. The date is the 27th of January. In paragraph 1 of this order, you say that there shouldn't be any offensive operations launched against the ABiH. What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wrote this document on the basis of a joint statement made by Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban on the 27th of January in Geneva, as we can see, where they said that the HVO and the BH Army could not fight each other. So I am warning the HVO, for my part, that it was not to undertake any offensive operations against the BH Army. On the other hand, Sefer Halilovic was to do the same, appealing to his units, until both of us met in Kiseljak 10 days later and endeavoured to tackle the problem in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P01 -- P01471. I have a couple of brief questions about it. It's a document that concerns a meeting between General Morillon, Halilovic, and yourself, and Siber; 11th of February, 1993. Do you remember this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The meeting was held in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On page 1, have a look at what Mr. Halilovic says. It's at the bottom of the page: "Halilovic." There it is. He says that their strategic interest is to find a solution with the HVO, and that this is also the interest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When I read that -- Halilovic was an important officer of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. When I read that, I told myself that it was perhaps one way of Halilovic recognising the existence of the HVO. That's what he says. He says it's in the interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So you, who knew Halilovic, do you think that this is in accordance with what he really thought? How would you interpret what he said on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes, he did say that, that the strategic interest was co-operation with the Croats, and this was linked to Mr. Izetbegovic's and Boban's letter of the 27th of January, where he says that joint commands must be established. And in that light and in that spirit, he says that it was truly in his interests that the Croats and Muslims should co-operate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The joint command was a notion that was addressed by a number of witnesses. Various Defence teams have referred to the solution, and I can see that Halilovic has also discussed the matter, because he says that. That would make it possible to prevent incidents from arising, the existence of a joint command would make that possible. As far as you know, was Mr. Halilovic of this opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did discuss the matter, and on that day we even established this joint staff of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, precisely on that day. We saw the order, we gave instructions, and set up this joint staff for the 3rd Corps and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. And there were two commanders at its head, Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you've mentioned Enver Hadzihasanovic. As you know, and it's no mystery for you, I was familiar with his case because one of the Defence counsel present in the courtroom was defending General Kubura. I remember that in the case I put certain questions, a lot of questions. And I remember that in the submissions before the Appeal Chamber, the Anglo-Saxon Defence asked the Appeals Chamber to say that a Judge should not put questions, and the Appeals Chamber said, Yes, it's part of a Judge's mission to put questions. And I'm reminding those of you who have forgotten this of the fact, and I invite you to read the judgement on this issue that was dealt with in the Hadzihasanovic case. I'm not going to discuss the Hadzihasanovic case, however. But the sentence that we can see before his name states the following: General Halilovic says there are extremists on both sides. What did he mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he meant was that there were certain groups of people who had some sort of their army of their own and who wanted, in their own way, to take part in everything that was happening, which meant that they were opposed to what the two commanders had agreed to. That means there were forces that were opposed to having the agreement signed and applied, and that's when they went into action and did what they wanted to destroy such an agreement or have it fail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll move on to P01558, which is a Prosecution document that has been admitted into evidence, and it has already been discussed. It's a letter sent to you by General Morillon, February 1993. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it, but I can't read it because I don't have it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Apparently, General Morillon spoke about the fact that in certain UNHCR vehicles, weapons were found, and he says that this should not be tolerated. Do you see? We have already dealt with this issue. General Praljak spoke to us about it, provided us with some explanations. As far as you know, were there humanitarian convoys that moved around occasionally with weapons inside the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Antonetti, Your Honour, there were quite a lot of complaints and criticisms of the behaviour of members of the UNHCR, particularly with respect to where vehicles which the UNHCR had mobilised, if I can use the word, from the local people who had their vehicles, and for a certain time they were paid for by the UNHCR for them to use it. And this would be found in vehicles that were locally owned and rented out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, have a look at the following document, P1988. It's a document that we have already seen. You signed it, Halilovic, Thebault, and Morillon. I'm waiting for it to appear on the screen. There it is. It's a Prosecution document, and this is the first time you're going to tell me something about this document because it's the first time I'm putting this direct question to you. And for me, this is an important document, and I would go as far as saying that it is a very important document. April 1993. You know that in the indictment, the month of April is a month that's linked to the ultimatum as well, but all the parties, the international community, yourself, and Halilovic, appear to be saying that the ABiH and the HVO are legal military forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and should be treated equally. So either I fold my arms and don't say anything, or I should intervene and ask you what your opinion is. So what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this observation in item 1 is completely true, and it was accepted by both sides because it had confirmation in the changes and amendments on the provisions governing the armed forces, and the agreement signed on friendship and co-operation, and in certain activities which were in the offing between Boban and Izetbegovic where they said that a joint command -- or joint commands should be established as being commands of a joint army. And I'd like to add to that that at this meeting also present were the vice-president or vice-premier, Granic -- vice-president of the Presidency, that is, and Mr. Kresimir Zubak, who was also vice-president of the HVO. Therefore, there was a good representation here, a good team which made this observation and confirmed that it wasn't something of the moment, but that it had deep roots, and that they were lagging behind in setting up these joint commands and commands at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A well-intentioned -- or ill-intentioned person could use this document to say that General Morillon signed this, and it was, in fact, to please General Petkovic, because what he wanted was to have a cease-fire. So to say that HVO is a legal army, well, it's not important. What's important is that General Petkovic is ordering a cease-fire, that there should be joint commissions, and so on, and to say that the HVO is a legal military force is of no interest. So what would you say if one objected in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm going to say is this: I'm going to present my view, and that is that on the 18th of April, Messrs. Izetbegovic and Boban contacted General Morillon and Mr. Thebault, and many other representatives of the United Nations, too, to place at the disposal of the BH Army and the HVO to prevent the conflicts and to help arrive at a solution that would result in a lasting peace in the area. They were conscious of that. They took on that role at the request of Mr. Izetbegovic and Boban. And you saw that Mr. Thebault came from Zagreb -- yes, from Zagreb, and that Benal [phoen] came from Sarajevo as well, and that General Morillon flew in from Sarajevo and brought General Halilovic with him. So they responded to this call from the two presidents to offer their high-ranking services to them. And, furthermore, based on this agreement, they placed their resources at their disposal, they pledged to place their resources at their disposal as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a look at document P02038. It's the following document in my list. It's a Prosecution document. You are the author of this document dated the 22nd of April. As you can see, I'm going back in time. It concerns how civilians and prisoners should be treated. Paragraph 1, you say it's necessary to respect and protect the civilian population affected by the war, and you add that they don't have an active role in the conflict and should, therefore, not be attacked. So why did you think it was useful to draft such an order, why?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you saw that I was with Halilovic on the 20th, and we were together on the 21st in Central Bosnia. And we spent two days touring every part of this area to size up the situation, and we said that we would both act urgently. Upon my return on the 22nd to Herzegovina or the Main Staff, on the basis of everything that I had seen and we had seen together, I sat down and wrote this warning to the units of the Croatian Defence Council, telling them how they should behave. On the 21st, I also held a meeting in Vitez, where I said that soldiers might be killed, but that civilians must not be killed, so there can be no justification for the killing of civilians. And soldiers went into action knowing that they might be killed. So on the basis of all the agreements we had reached, the information I had gathered, I was able to compile a demand of this kind, which I addressed to all units of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. We'll have a look at the following document, but it must be under seal because it is a document from the Canarias Tactical group. P02192. It shouldn't be shown to the outside. General Petkovic, so far all the documents -- all my questions have had to do with documents that have already been discussed here with other witnesses. They are documents that have been admitted. And all the subjects the documents deal with have already been dealt with, so I'm not referring to any new subjects. All these subjects have already been dealt with. I say that to respond to certain comments that were made a while ago. This document here, which was drafted by the Spaniards, I would like you to have a look at page 4 of the document, which is where you are referred to. At the very beginning, under A, there's a reference to the Mostar zone. It says that you and Lasic were heading towards Jablanica with 18 ambulances. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do. That's what was agreed, and that's how the HVO prepared itself and moved to Konjic and Jablanica. But it's not Lasic here. It should be Filipovic. They made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a mistake; fine. Thanks. At least my question has the merit of having resulted in the correction of an error. Under B, I wasn't going to ask you this question, but I remembered what General Praljak said. According to SpaBat, local newspapers carried news concerning the visit of a delegation from the Assembly of the Republic of Croatia, headed by Akmadzic, the premier of the BiH government. General Praljak told us that he had acted so that Croatian parliamentarians, members of the Assembly, could realise what the situation was like -- they could realise what the situation was like in the field. Do you remember the members of the Croatian Assembly coming to the area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did come, and I think they were led by - was it Mr. Seks? - and Mr. Akmadzic, as prime minister of the BH government, greeted the delegation of the BH Assembly, and mostly they stayed in the Mostar area. However, the conclusion was that they weren't able to see much. But they were down there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at the paragraph on Jablanica, and your name appears in that paragraph. The Spaniards stated that the village of Doljani was destroyed, houses were burnt down, that men had been taken to Sovici, that 60 elderly men were being detained in the school in Sovici. That's what the Spaniards say. Is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you saw, and we looked at the film, at the footage, that we decided to go to Sovici and Doljani, and you saw our whole journey to Sovici and Doljani. But SpaBat obviously didn't know what Sovici was and what Doljani was. We had passed through Sovici because the BH Army wasn't interested in Doljani.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or, We passed through Doljani. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we first stopped off at the exit to Doljani village, I don't remember what that hamlet is called. But, anyway, from the APC, I don't know what impression they gained from there about Doljani, but it is true that we reached the school building and that we visited the people who were in the classroom in the school, in one of the classrooms of the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One-but-last question. Look at the reference to Konjic, the last sentence, when the SpaBat says that according to information, Zuka and his men had killed 15 civilians and took 7 prisoners of the HVO, and they also killed some elderly people. This is a climate encountered by SpaBat, and this information, I assume, will go to those people in Geneva. So prisoners in Trusina, and he's also accused of having killed elderly people in Sultici. But this shows that there was combat, that there were civilians, that there were prisoners. What do you say about the role of Zuka, and did his role affect your own role?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were aware of this even earlier, and that is why we went with 15 ambulances to evacuate the wounded and the dead. Zuka played a major role here by preventing an HVO team coming in with all the ambulances and the SpaBat team, so we didn't enter the area between Kostajnica and Konjic. So all people who were there wounded, they remained there, and our 15 ambulances and 3 doctors returned to Mostar without having carried out their task, thanks to Zuka. And also there's Cibo who is not mentioned here, but he was there too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like you to look at the 41st Brigade. This is on page 5, but the last sentence, where the Spaniards talk about the Main Staff. It is "03.," the frequencies used by the Main Staff. When I saw this, I said to myself that the Spaniards must have had means to listen in to the BiH and the HVO. What do you think of that? Why are they giving the frequencies? If they are giving the frequencies, it's because they're tapping them. Or is there some other explanation?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the communications resources used by the HVO Bosnia-Herzegovina could be intercepted by anyone who wanted. The Spanish are a modern army, and they have the means to listen in to far more complicated equipment than Motorolas that were used by our policemen on the side of the ABiH and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen carefully to my question. I will repeat it. I saw this sentence. I don't know anything about it. If I had seen it when the Spaniards had come, I would have asked them the same question. However, by chance I discovered this phrase afterwards, subsequently. But if I had discovered this before they came, I would have asked the question, because if UNPROFOR is capable of listening in to frequencies used by ABiH, of which we have material proof here, and also to the HVO, this meant that they were normally informed about everything that was happening; for example, of the project and plans for the future. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they would have learnt much by listening in. There's something else here; that is, the SpaBat contingent in Jablanica. At any point in time when I went there, you could find 50 to 100 civilians who were freely walking around the Spanish Battalion compound, as opposed to Medjugorje, where not a single civilian could enter until he was met at the entrance and accompanied. This unit in Jablanica led their own way of life. Juka [as interpreted] had lived in Spain, he could speak Spanish, and in Jablanica there was a special rhythm and mode of life of the Spanish Battalion, so that in communicating amongst themselves, they learnt what they wanted to find out, and even more than that. The SpaBat unit in Jablanica was simply the least professional section of the Spanish Battalion, and I think that Zuka had the main say in their compound. There were even rumours about drugs being moved around and other things with respect to that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from what you're saying, should we conclude that regarding the Jablanica zone, the reports by UNPROFOR could be a subject of caution in view of the closeness between the ABiH, that is, Zuka, and the Spaniards?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know whether it has been admitted into evidence, but once I sent a very serious objection to Colonel Morales, and then I apologised and said that a member of the army had abused his hospitality and said that it was inappropriate for such a large number of members of the army and other civilians to be moving around in their compound, whereas when I go to Medjugorje, I am met at the entrance and then I am accompanied wherever I was going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have the break, and after that we'll come to document 02082.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two points. First of all, regarding the question of additional time for the cross-examination, the Chamber says that if there is a need for additional time, it will be up to the parties, when the time comes, to make a request. As the questions have not been completed, we have to wait for the end of the Judges' questions for you to ask for additional time. Secondly, a small point of precision regarding the question linked to the oral ruling of the Chamber on the scope of the additional examination. The last sentence, which explains that the Petkovic Defence may address subjects addressed by the Judges during the re-examination, and it is within that scope that the questions may be put. To respond to Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Khan, Mr. Scott, during the break I referred to the decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber in the Halilovic case. It would be very brief. I will refer to paragraph 84 of the judgement, and I read: "Halilovic supports that Dzemal was questioned by the Chamber during eight hours. The Appeals Chamber feels that the time devoted by the Judges to the questioning of the witness cannot lead to anyone making the conclusion of any prejudice." And the arguments are being rejected. Paragraph 102, listen carefully, because all this has already been covered: "The Appeals Chamber notes that in application of Rule 85(B) of the Rules, the Judge may also ask any question to the witness at any stage of the proceedings. The Judges may ask any questions which they consider to be necessary in order to clarify a point addressed during the testimony or throw light on the facts. They may also question witnesses on points which were not addressed by the parties." Similarly, the Judges may also ask an expert witness questions on subjects that are not covered in his report. That is what the Appeals Chamber has said, and I comply with the Appeals Chamber ruling. Thirdly, in the Hadzihasanovic case, the Appeals Chamber, which his counsel raised questions with the Appeals Chamber, the counsel of Hadzihasanovic, once again the Hadzihasanovic trial does not lead to any reasonable conclusion that the Judges have shown any prejudice, nor that anyone was penalised. Furthermore, in the Hadzihasanovic trial, there was no opposition to the questions by the Judges, and no objections were raised during the trial. Those were the questions that I put to General Petkovic, whether he wants me to continue with my questions or not. If he had said, No, I would have stopped. So please read the judgements of the Appeals Chamber before making any objections. General Petkovic, I'm now going to address the document that I mentioned a moment ago, which is again a document of the Spanish Battalion. And I wish to ask you to look at page 5, where reference is made to Zuka. It is in the paragraph referring to Jablanica. You said a moment ago that Zuka was very close to the Spanish Battalion, but here it appears that they are saying that there was combat which was the result of the renegade activities conducted by Zuka or armed gangs of his kind. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we knew and they are saying here that Zuka was in command of the so-called Black Swans. This was one of the worst units, if I may say so, operating in the territory of Konjic-Jablanica, and before that to a considerable extent in Sarajevo, and they were pulled out of there. And with Safet Cibo's arrival and Zuka's arrival, they were deployed in the Konjic/Jablanica area. And I'm not aware of other units commanded by Zuka. I know about this unit of Black Swans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us look at document P02182. I apologise for speeding things up, but there are many documents. If you're tired, tell me, General Petkovic. I do not wish to tire you. It's a document you're familiar with. You drafted it, and you're asking Stipe Pole to release civilians in Doljani and Sovici, but to keep those who can do their military service. When I read this sentence, I wondered whether General Petkovic wanted to select some of the men among the detainees, issue an order to release civilians who had nothing to do with this, but to keep civilians who were fit for military service who could be incorporated within the ABiH or the HVO. Did you make such distinctions or not?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as far as this document is concerned, I said that it had nothing to do with the document relating to the Main Staff. This form of document seems to have strayed to the set of documents that we have before us, because the Main Staff does not refer to the brigade or battalion; it places its own markings on the left-hand side and then addresses it to whoever it may be. And on the footage of the 4th, you saw that I was in the school with those people there and that I promised that all those people, by 4.00, would be sent home and relocated, and then there was a turn-about by which Halilovic and Pasalic asked for these people to be evacuated to the Jablanica area. So in that group of people, the group of people up there, Your Honours, you can't say, This man is military fit and this one is a civilian. All men who were able-bodied men on the 18th were transferred to detention, so all those who remained were civilians who, in one way or another, were placed under the -- under protection in the school in Sovici, so that you couldn't distinguish between the two, you couldn't separate them. And on the 5th, in the morning, all of them were evacuated. Nobody was held back anywhere. So that as far as this document is concerned, I cannot accept it as being my own document or a Main Staff document, because it has none of the features of a Main Staff document. If there were my signature, that would be another matter. But when I see what it says on the left-hand side, I just cannot accept it as being my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: You've been many times asked and requested by the President, by other colleagues, that you speak very fast, and sometimes when you read a document it really cannot be translated. Frankly, I would also ask the same question to other colleagues of ours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, if I understand this correctly, I'm trying to reach certain conclusions on the basis of what you're saying, but there are two hypothesis, and no more. Either it's a false document, and then we don't know who produced it, or it's someone from your surroundings who thought he was acting well by sending this document. Perhaps there are other possibilities, other hypotheses. I don't know. But you are saying that this isn't a document from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not about the Main Staff. Let me repeat. We dealt with the problem of people on the 4th of May and set out for Jablanica, and those people the very next day were evacuated. Nobody remained. None of the men remained. All those who were there were evacuated. So I see no reason, after giving my promise that people would leave, and asking Halilovic to evacuate everybody, that I would then write something like this, telling them to hold back people. And then, as I say, the next day everybody left, nobody remained. So this document, I don't know how to call it -- what to call it. And as I've said before, it has none of the markings of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I'd like to intervene with -- as far as the translation and transcript is concerned. The general said with respect to Halilovic's request to evacuate everybody, which means that Halilovic made this request that all the people be evacuated; and in the transcript it says "asking Halilovic to evacuate." And from that, it would follow that somebody asked Halilovic to evacuate the people. So, General, can you tell us again, who asked whom about the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Halilovic, after we left the school, asked that the evacuation of these people be carried out, that they be evacuated from Sovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, there are two documents that are almost identical, P02203 and P02200. These are documents -- well, the second one was drafted by you, and the first one was signed on your behalf. It has to do with [indiscernible], that I can see the word "green" in this document, the greens, the Muslims. A while ago, you said that you didn't use such derogatory terms for Muslims, and you only recognised one document. And the document that you recognised, it's the -- well, was that document 2200; is that the document that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 2200 and document 2203 are identical, they're one and the same document. As far as I can see, looking at the reference number, 728, 728, same thing, so it's exactly the same document, and it was just registered under two different numbers. But it's the same document. You saw Mr. Filipovic's statement, saying that he, in talking to the Main Staff, was the organiser of checking the arrival of the buses, so I did not draft this document. Mr. Filipovic, in talking to the Main Staff and discussing the issue, was prompted to write this document. When this document was being compiled in Mostar, I was in Jablanica. The 5th of May. I was in Jablanica on the 5th of May. And you were able to see, during Filipovic's testimony, that he called up Mostar to check about the vehicles, so this document was written in Mostar. I was in Jablanica, which is, after all, 70 kilometres away, and somebody signed for the chief of the Main Staff. But without my signature, who that was, I assume the original -- on the original, you can see who actually signed it in lieu of me. So I'm not the author of this document. And you had witness statements -- the statement of a witness who helped write this document. And the document emanated from Mostar, and Petkovic at that time was in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a look at the following document, P02344. We've seen this document already on numerous occasions. We've seen it, we've put questions to witnesses about it. But you are sitting before me. As you signed the document, it would be quite strange if I didn't put questions to you about it. Have a look at Article 4 to save time. You say that prisoners should be released, and all the civilian detainees should be released, without any conditions. The fact that civilian detainees was referred to might lead the Judge to conclude that this is material evidence that shows that you are aware of the fact that there were detained civilians, which is in violation of International Humanitarian Law, but there might be other reasons. The fact that one has drafted this means that one is aware of the consequences. Perhaps the lawyer didn't notice all the problems, Although I hadn't studied international law, et cetera. There could be reasons for this. So when you discussed the matter with Halilovic and Morillon and Thebault, the issue of civilians prisoners, what did they know about that issue, and what did you know about the issue?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already said that the civilians were evacuated to Heliodrom and that they were taken in by the civilian structures there. So that is my position. And in taking that position, I do not start out from the fact that anybody detained those people. I confronted the situation in negotiations and talks, because others asked that this term be introduced. Halilovic also wanted this term to be introduced. And there was a discussion on that point, and I was not able to make any other conclusion and say that I distanced myself from that. And as I said, the document was compiled by representatives of SpaBat, which doesn't mean that I didn't read the document, that I hadn't read the document before I signed. But, anyway, regardless of the fact that it is my signature, I don't stand by the fact that they were civilian detainees or prisoners, because they weren't received by any institution taking in prisoners, but by welfare people dealing with social welfare --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: {Interpretation] -- regardless of the fact that that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whose idea was it to use the English word "detainees" here?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document came into being after our talks in the operative section of SpaBat, the operations section of SpaBat. Two or three of their officers took part, and, according to a cliche, well, it's the kind of format and way in which all agreements were written at the time. And this is a short version of that, and I signed it, among other things. But I don't stand by that, nor ever will, regardless of how you interpret it, were they detainees or prisoners, or whatever, because there weren't any people -- they were taken care of by the civilian sector in Herzegovina throughout.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have a look at P02492. In the middle of the first page -- it's not on the screen yet, but you have it, so you can save time. In the middle of the first page, it says that in the period from December 1992 to mid-March 1993, there are two parallel governments in existence in Jablanica, a Croatian one and a Muslim one, which apparently co-operated with each other. Is that the conclusion you, yourself, reached?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I knew that there was the Crisis Staff in Jablanica municipality until Safet Cibo arrived, I knew about the participation of Croats in that Crisis Staff, but I also knew that the HVO existed; of Jablanica, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. P02856. The date is the 20th of June, 1993, and it has to do with placing -- implementing a cease-fire which you signed with Adzic and Dezic [as interpreted] in the presence of Walgren, Thornberry, and Morillon. Do you remember this agreement on a cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do. It is the agreement of the 15th of June, 1993, at Sarajevo Airport, signed by the three parties in the presence of Mr. Walgren, Thornberry, and, of course, Morillon as the host for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, you've seen a series of documents on cease-fires. There's a cease-fire, and then fighting resumes. Then there's another cease-fire, and it resumes again. I won't start discussing about who resumed the fighting. I'm not at that stage. But I'd like to know the following: The members of the international community, such as Walgren and Morillon, weren't they fed up with acting as go-betweens between the sides involved? Didn't they ask you, General Petkovic, why did it start again? And you'd say, The others started it again. When they saw Halilovic or Delic and asked them, Why did you resume the fighting? And they said, Well, it was the others who resumed the fighting. Well, how, in fact, did the members of the international community perceive the situation? Because we constantly see orders stating that cease-fires should be implemented. So to complete my question, because in the Prosecution's submissions there are certain elements, and I have to provide you with all the elements so that you can respond. I don't want to hide anything from you. The Prosecution states that there was a hypocritical attitude, you said for the sake of the international community that there would be a cease-fire, but in fact you had no intention of acting in that way. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would put it the other way around. But linked to this meeting, let me say that General Walgren came to Sarajevo, and on the 15th of June there was a meeting in Geneva. Mr. Izetbegovic left the meeting here and returned from the meeting. We signed an agreement on the 15th of June simultaneously, and this was the time when Travnik fell, and Kakanj in Central Bosnia fell, too, so I wouldn't be two-faced, would I, and say that I liked having the BH Army take control of Travnik and Kakanj, and for the fact that 25.000 to 30.000 Croats had been expelled. So this document is linked to the events on the ground, that is to say, the fall of Travnik and the fall of Kakanj in Central Bosnia, or, rather, the BH Army taking control of both places and expelling that number of Croats. And I said, Check it out, and we'll see whether it happened or not, and then we can see who is playing a double game or is two-faced here in all these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that you have to see who the hypocrite was. But you are saying that, in any event, if I have understood you correctly, you are not the hypocrite. General Petkovic, I'm putting these questions to you because, according to the Rules, it is my obligation to determine the truth. It's Article 9 -- it's Rule 90 of the Rules. When I put questions to a witness, I have to determine the truth. It's a moral obligation, and this is the reason for which, when I see an entire series of orders on the implementation of cease-fires, and I then see that the fighting resumes, and then there is a new cease-fire, when I see such a situation, I try to determine what the truth is. It's not just a matter for the Prosecution and the Defence. This is my role, too, to establish what the truth is, as pointed out by the Appeals Chamber in the paragraph that I read out a minute ago, a while ago. So if I have understood you correctly, you're saying that as far as you are concerned, there was no double game, no two-faced attitude. Have a look at P02950. It's from the International Red Cross, and it concerns prisoners. It's addressed to Mr. Blaskic. The date is the 25th of June, 1993. And the International Red Cross says that it is preoccupied by the issue of detainees, of prisoners. Were you familiar with this document at the time, or did Colonel Blaskic never mention it to you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, linked to the agreement of the 15th of June, commissions were activated in Central Bosnia, and our commission, I think, was led by Pero Skopljak. I don't know who led the BH Army commission or, rather, who headed the Serb commission, because it was included in all that as well. And those commissions, after the 15th of June, tackled problems from Travnik to Kakanj, including Kiseljak, Kresevo, Vitez, so the whole area of Central Bosnia, in actual fact. And there is a report from that commission. I don't have it before me now, so I can't comment on what the specific items were. But after the agreement of the 15th of June, the commissions went out into the field to do their work, and you can see that in the previous order which said that the commissions would be set up and would start working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Petkovic, we will have to adjourn now because it's time. I have a few more documents to deal with with regard to the first day, what I call the first day. As I say, I'm following a certain chronology. The following documents will concern the 17th of July, 1993. But so that you can be more efficient tomorrow, I encourage you to read P07475 in its entirety, which is the summary of a meeting between Tudjman, Susak, and Bobetko. I've already mentioned this, and you are referred to it. Please read it carefully, because I checked and noticed that the Prosecution asked a question about the document, but it concerned one part of the document, and in my opinion there are other questions that could be raised. Read it carefully - you have ample time to do so before appearing here tomorrow - because I have a series of questions I'd like to put to you about the document. Once I have completed dealing with the items on this list, I'll start dealing with the "Defence," in inverted commas, documents. There are 30 of those documents, the numbers of which I provided this morning. The Registrar will ensure that we have the two videos at our disposal. It won't take much time, because it's a purely technical matter. I wish you a pleasant afternoon, and I will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of February, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
